## Proof

Let $\mathbf{x}=(x,y,z)$ and $\boldsymbol{\xi}(\tau)=(\phi(\tau),\psi(\tau),\chi(\tau))$. Identify $D=a^{2}$ (the diffusion coefficient). Define the 3D heat kernel (fundamental solution of $\partial_{s}v=D\nabla^{2}v$):

$$\Phi(\mathbf{x},s)=\frac{1}{(4\pi Ds)^{3/2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{|\mathbf{x}|^{2}}{4Ds}\right),\qquad s>0.$$

Since $(2\sqrt{\pi D})^{3}=8\pi^{3/2}D^{3/2}=(4\pi D)^{3/2}$, the given function is exactly

$$u(\mathbf{x},t)=\int_{0}^{t}f(\tau)\,\Phi\!\big(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\xi}(\tau),\,t-\tau\big)\,d\tau. \tag{$\ast$}$$

The heat kernel satisfies, for $s>0$,
$$\partial_{s}\Phi=D\nabla^{2}\Phi, \qquad \Phi(\cdot,s)\xrightarrow[s\to0^{+}]{}\delta \ \text{(in distributions)}.$$

### Initial condition

As $t\to0^{+}$, the domain of integration $[0,t]$ collapses and the integrand is locally integrable (with $f$ bounded near $0$), so

$$\lim_{t\to0^{+}}u(\mathbf{x},t)=0.$$

Thus $u\big|_{t=0}=0$, satisfying (2).

### PDE — differentiating $(\ast)$ in $t$

The variable $t$ enters both through the upper limit and through $s=t-\tau$. By the Leibniz rule (valid distributionally):

$$\partial_{t}u=\underbrace{f(t)\,\Phi\!\big(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t),\,0\big)}_{\text{boundary term}}+\int_{0}^{t}f(\tau)\,\partial_{s}\Phi\!\big(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\xi}(\tau),\,t-\tau\big)\,d\tau.$$

**Boundary term.** As $s\to0^{+}$, $\Phi(\cdot,s)\to\delta$, hence

$$\Phi\!\big(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t),\,0\big)=\delta\!\big(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\xi}(t)\big)=\delta(x-\phi(t))\,\delta(y-\psi(t))\,\delta(z-\chi(t)),$$

so the boundary term equals $f(t)\,\delta(x-\phi(t))\delta(y-\psi(t))\delta(z-\chi(t))$.

**Integral term.** Using $\partial_{s}\Phi=D\nabla^{2}\Phi$ and pulling the spatial Laplacian (acting on $\mathbf{x}$, which equals the Laplacian acting on the first argument of $\Phi$) out of the integral:

$$\int_{0}^{t}f(\tau)\,\partial_{s}\Phi\,d\tau=D\!\int_{0}^{t}f(\tau)\,\nabla^{2}_{\mathbf{x}}\Phi\,d\tau=D\,\nabla^{2}\!\int_{0}^{t}f(\tau)\,\Phi\,d\tau=D\,\nabla^{2}u=a^{2}\nabla^{2}u.$$

(The interchange of $\nabla^{2}$ with the integral is justified for $t-\tau>0$ on the open interval; the only singularity is at $\tau=t$, which is exactly the boundary term already extracted.)

### Conclusion

Combining both terms,

$$\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=a^{2}\!\left(\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial x^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial y^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial z^{2}}\right)+f(t)\,\delta(x-\phi(t))\,\delta(y-\psi(t))\,\delta(z-\chi(t)),$$

which is precisely equation (1), together with $u\big|_{t=0}=0$ from (2). Therefore the displayed integral is the solution of the Cauchy problem. $\blacksquare$
